acceptedReports.program: Community health access, cancer navigation and hepatitis screening

acceptance.evidence: Independent root original-source and signed ledger reconstruction: docs/geography-discovery/la-vacf-root-acceptance-20261005.md

what: Vital Access Care Foundation offers Vietnamese-language cancer and hepatitis screening, navigation and patient support in Orange County, inside the LA metro area.
It also connects residents to food, insurance and public-benefit services; its 2024 return reports 2,499 mixed screening/vaccination activities and 282 cancer patients assisted.
It helps residents navigate medical care in their own language, including hepatitis B services where timely follow-up can prevent serious liver disease.
strengths: Bilingual screening and navigation can turn an otherwise missed infection into monitoring, treatment or vaccination.
An established local service network reaches residents facing language and access barriers; completed care has a credible clinical mechanism.
Original returns establish a real operating recipient, and the historical community study supports a relevant hepatitis burden.
reservations: Current unique hepatitis tests, completed treatment and incremental cancer-stage outcomes are not reported.
The clinical transfer and resource ledger are explicit judgments; partner, public-payer and other portfolio effects remain unpriced.
Large unrestricted reserves and recent surpluses leave the next ordinary gift's service expansion uncertain.

sections.what: The [current programs](https://www.vacf.org/programs) include cancer and hepatitis screening, care navigation, medication assistance, peer support, food distribution and public-benefit enrollment. The [current organization page](https://www.vacf.org/about) locates services in Fountain Valley, Orange County, within the current LA–Long Beach–Anaheim metro boundary. The legal recipient is Vital Access Care Foundation dba Vietnamese American Cancer Foundation, EIN 91-2170415; the official site links its donation route.
sections.monitoring: The 2024 return reports 2,499 combined screenings/vaccinations and 282 cancer patients assisted; these are outputs, not lives saved. The current website's 2025 impact heading links an image whose filename still says 2024; the image shows 3,750 screening/prevention activities. We use the dated return cohort, not that ambiguously labeled image, for numerical scale. VACF's [2019 HBV study](https://www.vacf.org/_files/ugd/dd68d6_5174bf64856744a4af4985d3f0c2c316.pdf) found 225 current infections among 2,508 participants but explicitly lacked information on completed necessary care. Improved monitoring would publish unique tests by disease, prior diagnosis, confirmatory results, referral completion and treatment/vaccination outcomes. No current controlled cancer-stage, completed HBV-treatment or additional-income outcome was verified. Screening, infectious testing and vaccination totals cannot be treated as unique completed treatment. For the conditional reference, 25% of mixed activities are judged HBV opportunities and 80% unique service participants; their appropriateness is separately stress-tested. No raw screen is valued as a life saved.
sections.qualitative: Bilingual outreach and navigation can reduce missed diagnoses and improve linkage. The [Chahal clinical model](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6346293/) gives 23.861 discounted lifetime QALYs for the inclusive Asian/Pacific-Islander offer versus 23.780 without intervention: 0.081, not the table's sequential 0.007. This is modeled clinical evidence, not a VACF evaluation. Its disease progression, treatment response and finite lifetime are included once; no recurring lifetime copies or survivor earnings are added. The retained 0.25 transfer prior covers age/cascade mismatch and is not an observed treatment-completion probability. [CDC screening guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/rr/rr7201a1.htm) supports screening linked to appropriate care, but ordinary medical access is an alternative. [Every Woman Counts](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/services/every-woman-counts/) supplies free eligible breast/cervical screening and treatment referrals, including Vietnamese-language assistance; VACF cannot claim all partner-paid care as its additional effect. Broader cancer support, food security, research and training remain unknown rather than assigned arbitrary health or wage values.
sections.cost:
Original 2024 full-recipient expenses are $2,205,208: $2,153,424 program, $49,846 management and $1,938 fundraising. Separately netted event costs are zero; no rental, gaming or inventory expense addback was found. The 2022–24 expense mean is $1,531,013.33, used only as a cost sensitivity, not matched historical outputs. The annual-funded-work equivalent assigns 25% capacity expansion to an ordinary gift, giving 124.95 incremental service people; all incur modeled costs even if care or clinical benefit fails. Health remains 1.2018628125 LA QALYs. Signed household resources subtract 0.1312803504 welfare equivalents, yielding 1.0705824621 combined equivalents and $20.60 million per ten, versus the initial diagnostic's $18.35 million health-only estimate. A $10,000 gift corresponds to about 0.5666 incremental service people, 0.00545 clinical QALYs and −0.0005953 income equivalents, conditional on linear capacity. This is a partial recipient-funded component, not complete social EV or a marginal-gift queue observation.

Resource branches are mutually exclusive household outcomes, not separately added gains for the same family. The central reference assumes one unique service participant per distinct household and weights one welfare person per household. Other family-member welfare is unpriced; no conversion of unique participants into households by dividing by family size is used. Household baseline disposable resources are judged $30,000, compatible with—not estimated by—the historical low-income population. Every incremental screening household incurs $50 net time/travel cost. A 12.5% resource-care branch has $300 net resource relief or baseline-alive work preservation, discounted for 50% positive health overlap, minus $200 treatment/work disruption and the full $50 common cost: −$100. A disjoint 5% false-alarm branch loses $250; the remaining 82.5% loses $50. Taxes, benefit withdrawal, avoided bills, work disruption and replacement care must be netted inside these amounts; they are not measured separate gains. One household-year is counted, never survivor wages. Partner-payer stress separately assigns $1,459 or $5,000 per reference-equivalent clinical offer across 100 disjoint payer persons at $50,000 baseline, as one-year fiscal opportunity-cost losses. The $1,459 is the external model's inclusive-versus-no-intervention medical-cost difference, not current VACF costs or observed taxpayer incidence; fiscal opportunity cost and incidence are unknown in central. Three-year stress means recurrent care costs and resources each year, not repeated one-time screening cost asserted as fact. Private-provider margin and insurer/public-payer incidence are unknown, not factual zero; ±$25 per service counterparty stresses use ten disjoint one-person owner households at $60,000 baseline. Other local/nonlocal patient and partner burdens are unpriced. Thus the headline is explicitly partial, not total household resources or complete world benefit.
sections.funding: The [2024 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/912170415/202523219349307047/full) reports revenue of $3,252,848, a $1,047,640 surplus, $4,035,365 cash and $4,049,616 net assets without donor restrictions. Government grants are blank in Part VIII, which does not prove absence of publicly supported partner care. The [program page](https://www.vacf.org/programs) explicitly connects patients to Every Woman Counts and other assistance. An ordinary gift may support the entire expanded portfolio or reserves; no verified cash-only service queue was found. Funding responsiveness is therefore a judgment, not an observed grant-to-treatment conversion. The 25% capacity response is a donor-response prior, not observed additional patients per dollar. Zero expansion has no new benefits or service costs; clinical null retains all new service burdens.

model.costScope: Full annual recipient expenses / conditional incremental annual service capacity; partner clinical costs outside donor numerator and incompletely priced on social ledger.
model.geographicAttribution: 95% judged beneficiary residence in LA–Long Beach–Anaheim MSA, including Orange County; not allocated from office alone. All-population health separately serialized.
model.formula: S=N*HBVshare*uniqueShare*capacityShare; Qall=(S*appropriateShare*additionalCare*clinicalTransfer*qRef − S*additionalUnmodeledHarm)/(1+r)^delay; QLA=g*Qall. Each disjoint household branch nets positiveOverlap*resourceGain−full costs BEFORE log; income=.5*persons*discounted finite years*log(1+net/baseline)*g. Price10=10*C/(QLA+signed income).
model.counterfactual: Ordinary care and public programs may supply screening/treatment without this gift. additionalCare=.5 and capacityShare=.25 are distinct alternative-care and donor-capacity judgments. clinicalTransfer=.25 adjusts external offer evidence, not repeated funding attribution.
model.attribution: s and d translate mixed reported outputs to candidate clinical opportunities; no multiplying 9% prevalence into a reference model that already includes infection prevalence. t is a joint transfer discount for older case mix and less complete care than reference; not an empirically calibrated completion probability. No independent cancer/food/navigation additions that could double-count the same people.
model.uncertainty: Conditional reference, not calibrated posterior or complete portfolio EV. Unknown clinical/resource cases remain null; null clinical preserves signed resources.
model.nativeOutcomes: Conditional annual capacity: 124.95 unique service participants and judged appropriate opportunities; 62.475 additional-care offers before external transfer; 15.61875 reference-offer equivalents. These are modeled counts, not observed completed treatment. LA clinical health1.2018628125 QALYs; signed resource welfare−0.13128035042786065 equivalents.

historicalAlphaModel.costScope: Full recipient annual 2024 Part IX expense, all programs/overhead; no selected-program denominator. Output denominator prices only HBV screening/care contribution. External clinical costs excluded and discussed separately.
historicalAlphaModel.geographicAttribution: LA MSA comprises Los Angeles and Orange counties. Historical study events were in both and current service focus is Orange County. g=.95 is judgment allowing nonresident beneficiaries, range .9–1, not measured residence share. National research spillovers are unpriced.
historicalAlphaModel.formula: Q_all=N*s*d*a*b*t*q_ref; Q_LA=g*Q_all; price=10*C/Q_LA. N=2499 mixed screening/vaccination activities; s=.25 HBV-related screening opportunities; d=.8 unique appropriate people; a=.5 incremental versus other care; b=.25 ordinary-funding responsiveness; t=.25 age/cascade transfer; q_ref=23.861−23.780=.081 discounted lifetime QALY per API screening-program offer from Chahal et al. Central Q_all=1.26511875 and Q_LA=1.2018628125. One annual-budget cohort only; never repeat lifetime benefit each year.
historicalAlphaModel.counterfactual: Without additional ordinary funding, existing grants/reserves and public/clinical providers continue. a removes HBV care that would occur anyway; b removes non-marginal funding or displacement. The reference model's no-intervention comparator is more favorable than contemporary care, so it is not copied directly.
historicalAlphaModel.attribution: s and d translate mixed reported outputs to candidate clinical opportunities; no multiplying 9% prevalence into a reference model that already includes infection prevalence. t is a joint transfer discount for older case mix and less complete care than reference; not an empirically calibrated completion probability. No independent cancer/food/navigation additions that could double-count the same people.
historicalAlphaModel.uncertainty: All organization-specific conversion factors are explicit subjective scenarios, not measured rates or confidence intervals. Partial component only. Low/high combine assumptions rather than statistical bounds; zero and small adverse effects remain possible.
historicalAlphaModel.nativeOutcomes: Central 624.75 candidate HBV activities, 499.8 unique appropriate opportunities, 249.9 incremental opportunities before funding, 62.475 funding-responsive opportunities and 15.61875 reference-program-equivalent offers. These fractional expected quantities are model constructs, not observed diagnoses, cures or beneficiaries.

inputs.rationale: Published modeled (not empirical) API inclusive 23.861 minus no intervention 23.780; includes imperfect uptake, avoids inflating per actual test.

inputs.name: g
inputs.rationale: Local service focus with nonresident allowance; not office-location allocation.

sensitivity: Positive low/high prices span about $968.38m to $815,478 per 10 LA QALYs; zero incremental funding or completed care makes price nonfinite.
At $1m/10, full annual cost needs 22.05208 LA QALYs; at $100k/10 it needs 220.5208. Central component supplies 1.20186, so unpriced benefits or better conversion would have to close a large gap.

q_ref embeds finite survival, disease recurrence/progression, treatment discontinuation and 3% annual discount in the source model. It is not 0.081 QALYs per year and receives no extra lifetime multiplier.

A societal-cost sensitivity must add actual incremental antiviral/vaccine/monitoring resources, not copy the source's outdated $798/month branded tenofovir cost. No current payer cost is estimated here.
Using all 3,750 ambiguously year-labeled website activities as 2025 outputs would raise scale 50%, but cannot establish HBV mix or 2025 costs; not the central case.
